title: Eyes and ears
hookLine: the impurity of the eyes is coveting, of the ears is gossip (Asa di Var, ang 472)

lines: A SMALL WANT, A SMALL TASTE FOR RUMOR.
TWO DOORS IT CAME IN THROUGH.
cards: Scroll for ten minutes and count what comes in. Someone's new kitchen. Someone's vacation.
A car you can't afford. A rumor about a person you've never met, and three hundred comments about it. None of it touched your hands.

You didn't say a word. And yet the phone goes down with something new in it: a small want for what's theirs, a small taste for the rumor. Long before any feed, Guru Nanak named the two doors those come in through.

teach.b: Here's the rest of the salok on ang 472, in paraphrase. The sootak of the eyes is looking with desire at another's spouse, another's wealth, another's beauty.

The sootak of the ears is taking in slander, feeding on gossip. And the last line: Nanak, even those who seem like swans, pure and bright, are bound and led away, if they carry these. Look how exact this is.
The eyes aren't impure for seeing. They're impure for a certain kind of looking: the look that wants what belongs to someone else. Coveting.
It's quiet. Nobody else can see it.

teach.h: IT CHANGES THE ONE WHO DOES IT.
teach.b: But it changes the one doing it, because every look that wants another's life makes your own life look smaller. The ears aren't impure for hearing, either. Gurbani is meant to be heard, sung aloud as kirtan.

The impurity is in what the ears are fed. The salok's word for it is laaitbaaree: talebearing, backbiting, the tale carried about someone who isn't there. The salok pictures the ears almost eating it.
And gossip, like coveting, doesn't need you to do anything. You only have to listen, and enjoy it a little.

teach.h: FOUR DOORS: MIND, TONGUE, EYES, EARS.
teach.b: Put yesterday and today together and you have four doors: mind, tongue, eyes, ears. Greed, lies, coveting, gossip. Guru Nanak's point across all of it is the same.
Keeping these four doors clean is the real purity, and it happens many times a day, in moments nobody else will ever see.

how: Sikhs hear this salok of the four impurities in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching counts avoiding slander and coveting as part of daily discipline.

o: a loud quarrel out in the street
looking with desire at others' things

games.q: the four doors — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says the eyes are impure for seeing anything at all
the impurity is a certain look: wanting another's spouse, wealth or beauty.
the salok's word for what the ears take in is slander, talebearing
laaitbaaree: the tale carried about someone who isn't there.
Gurbani is meant to be heard; the impurity is in what the ears are fed.

games.q: your friends start sharing a juicy rumor about someone who isn't in the room. what does the salok call this?
games.why: the sootak of the ears is taking in slander. it doesn't need you to do anything; you only have to listen and enjoy it.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something simple, a wall, a cup, the sky, and just see it, without wanting or judging. Then close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you, just hearing them, without a story.
If you pray, let Waheguru be the one word you listen to inside.

wordCard.voice: Laaitbaaree, talebearing or backbiting: in Guru Nanak's salok, the eyes' impurity is coveting what is another's; the ears' impurity, laaitbaaree, is feeding on gossip.

carryVoice: Your line: clean eyes, clean ears. Four doors, kept clean in moments nobody sees. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (man kaa sootak lobh hai), Ang 472
